sections.h2: What counts as a homestead for Alabama property tax?
sections.html:
For tax purposes, the Alabama Department of Revenue defines a homestead as a single-family, owner-occupied dwelling and the land that goes with it, up to 160 acres. The owner has to live there as a primary residence on the first day of the tax year for which the exemption is requested.

That wording matters for anyone planning a sale. A house that sits empty after a move, a rental, or a home held by heirs who live elsewhere does not fit the plain description. A house the owner lives in does, and the owner may qualify for a reduction in assessed value or, for some older and disabled owners, a larger break.

The department publishes its homestead page and points owners to the Code of Alabama, Title 40, sections 9-19 through 9-21, for the legal text. It also posts yearly memoranda that explain the federal and state income tests used for the income-limited types.

sections.h2: Which homestead types does Alabama list, and who gets each one?
sections.html:
Alabama sorts homestead relief into four named types, labeled H-1 through H-4, set out under Act 2013-295. Age, income and disability decide which one applies to a given owner.

TypeWho it is forWhat the department says it does
H-1Owners under 65 who are not disabled$4,000 of assessed value on the state portion and $2,000 of assessed value on the county portion
H-2Owners 65 or older with adjusted gross income under $12,000 on the latest state return, or owners retired because of permanent and total disabilityExempt from the state portion, plus $5,000 of assessed value on the county portion, school district tax included
H-3 (age 65+)Owners 65 or older with net taxable income of $12,000 or less on the combined federal returnExempt from all ad valorem taxes
H-3 (disabled)Owners who are permanently and totally disabledExempt from all ad valorem taxes, with no income limit
H-4Owners 65 or older with income above $12,000 on the latest Alabama returnExempt from the state portion and given the regular $2,000 assessed-value exemption on county taxes

Notice that the figures are assessed values, not market values. Because Alabama assesses residential property at a fraction of market value, an exemption of a few thousand dollars of assessed value removes a much larger slice of the house price from the tax base.

sections.h2: How do the state, county and school pieces of the bill differ?
sections.html:
Alabama homestead relief is applied separately to the state, county and school district parts of the bill, which is why two neighbors of different ages can see very different results.

The department's tables show the pattern. Owners who are not 65 receive up to $4,000 of assessed value off the state tax, and no income limit applies. Owners 65 or older, owners with a permanent and total disability, and blind owners have no maximum assessed value on the state exemption, again with no income limit and the same 160-acre ceiling.

The county side is more varied. The department notes that counties, municipalities or other taxing authorities may grant a homestead exemption of up to $4,000 in assessed value, and that county school tax is collected on some categories and not on others. The result is a patchwork that depends on the county and on the owner. A seller who wants to know what a buyer will pay should call the local assessing office rather than assume the statewide minimum.

sections.h2: Where do you apply for the Alabama homestead exemption?
sections.html:
You apply at your local county office, not with the state. The Department of Revenue says plainly to visit the county office where the home sits, and its FAQ repeats that all property tax other than public utility property is assessed and collected through the 67 county tax offices.

  • Expect to show that you own the house and live in it as your primary residence.
  • If you are claiming the age-based types, expect to show your age and, where the type has an income limit, the tax return the department's memorandum names.
  • If you are claiming disability, the department posts a physician's affidavit that a doctor uses to verify permanent and total disability.
  • Ask the office which type it has on file for you.

The department lists county office contacts on its site, and the Property Tax Division can be reached at 334-242-1525 if you cannot tell which office handles your parcel.

sections.h2: What does the principal residence exemption add?
sections.html:
Alabama also has a combined state, county and city principal residence exemption under Title 40, section 9-21. It covers two groups: owners 65 or older with income of no more than $12,000 on the combined federal return, and owners who are permanently and totally disabled regardless of age.

For both groups the department lists no maximum assessed value, a land limit of 160 acres, and no collection of county school tax. The disabled category has no income limit. The relief closely matches what the H-3 type describes.

sections.h2: What happens to the exemption when you sell the house?
sections.html:
The department's page does not say what happens to an exemption in the middle of a year when ownership changes, so a seller should not guess. The only rule the page states is the occupancy test: the owner must live in the home as a primary residence on the first day of the tax year.

That test points to a practical split. If you owned and lived in the house on that date, the exemption question for that year turned on your occupancy, and a buyer who moves in later starts the process with the county office. A buyer who plans to rent the house or flip it will not meet the occupancy test, so an investor should price the property at the tax level without an exemption.

  • Ask the county office how a sale date affects your current-year bill.
  • Check the payoff or title company statement for how property tax is split between seller and buyer.
  • Keep your copy of the exemption approval in case the title company asks for it.

sections.h2: What if you inherited a house and are thinking about selling?
sections.html:
An heir who does not live in the inherited house does not meet the department's occupancy wording, so the decedent's exemption should not be assumed to continue. If the previous owner was 65 or older and paid little or no tax, the first bill after the death can look much higher.

Plan for that. Taxes are due October 1 and delinquent after December 31, according to the department, and the County Revenue Commissioner is not required to mail tax notices. A bill that goes unpaid during a slow estate can turn into a larger problem, so check the account with the county as early as you can.

Heirs who want to skip repairs, carrying costs and uncertainty sometimes choose to sell as-is. A cash buyer can close on your timeline and handle the cleanup, which is one way to stop the tax clock running against you. You can compare options at your own pace, and you owe nothing if you decline an offer.

sections.h2: Which dates should a seller track each year?
sections.html:
Four dates drive most homestead and tax decisions in Alabama: October 1, December 31, January 1 and the date you list or sign a contract. The department publishes a short timetable for the tax cycle.

WhenWhat happens
October 1Taxes are due
January 1Taxes are delinquent
FebruaryDelinquent accounts go to the probate court
MarchProbate court meets
AprilProperty is advertised for sale
MayTax sale

A homestead exemption lowers the amount owed but does not move any of these dates.

Yes, in one respect. The department says owners of manufactured homes who are over 65 are exempt from the registration fee on an owner-occupied manufactured home, but they still pay the $5 issuance fee.

That is separate from the homestead types above, and it matters if you are selling a mobile or manufactured home on land you own. Ask the county office which fees and exemptions apply to the home itself and which apply to the land, since the two can be billed differently.

faqs.q: Who qualifies for the Alabama homestead exemption?
faqs.a: An owner of a single-family home who lives in it as a primary residence on the first day of the tax year, on up to 160 acres. The amount depends on age, income and disability status, and the department lists types H-1 through H-4.

faqs.q: Is there an age requirement for the largest exemption?
faqs.a: The biggest breaks go to owners 65 or older, permanently and totally disabled owners, and in some state categories blind owners. The H-3 type for people 65 or older also has an income limit of $12,000 on the combined federal return, while the disabled H-3 type has no income limit.

faqs.q: How much is the basic exemption for owners under 65?
faqs.a: The department lists $4,000 of assessed value on the state portion and $2,000 of assessed value on the county portion for H-1 owners. Counties and other taxing authorities may grant up to $4,000 of assessed value on their own.

faqs.q: Do I apply with the state or the county?
faqs.a: You apply at your county office. The Department of Revenue publishes the rules, but county offices assess and collect the tax.

faqs.q: When are Alabama property taxes due?
faqs.a: The department says property taxes are due October 1 and are delinquent after December 31. The County Revenue Commissioner does not have to mail a bill, so you owe the tax whether or not a statement arrives.

faqs.q: Can I keep my homestead exemption after I sell?
faqs.a: The department's page does not address a mid-year sale. A buyer must apply at the county office, and the occupancy test looks at who lives in the home on the first day of the tax year.
